name: sidebar
description:
A persistent index beside the content. 11 uses across the app and the website.

The part always got wrong is not the look — it is that a sidebar which becomes a drawer on a narrow viewport is still ONE navigation landmark, and duplicating it as a second hidden copy makes a screen reader announce two.

What the look has to do is quieter than it sounds: an index is read by scanning, so it needs a rhythm rather than decoration. Sections that group, a rule that separates without shouting, a current item that is unmistakable at a glance, and a footer that sits at the bottom rather than after the last link. It was a flat slab with three words floating in it.

base.$description:
CONTAINER. This unit establishes an inline-size container named after itself, so anything inside it can respond to the width of THIS BOX rather than to the width of the window. That is the difference that matters for a design system: a composite dropped into a 320px sidebar and the same composite on a 320px phone are the same situation, and a viewport query calls them different ones. The library carries no viewport media query anywhere for exactly this reason — the only `@media` in it is `prefers-reduced-motion`, which is a person's setting and not a size.

`inline-size: 16rem` with `max-inline-size: 100%`, and the split matters. It was `78vw` — a docked sidebar measuring the window, a box it does not live in. `min(16rem, 100%)` fixed the viewport half and broke the layout half: in a grid track sized `auto`, `100%` resolves against a track being sized BY this element, which is circular and lands on zero. The docs rail vanished entirely.

A DEFINITE width with a cap does both jobs: 16rem in an auto track, and shrinking to fit when the parent is genuinely narrower. This is the second time this exact circularity has cost a layout, and both times the symptom was a whole element gone rather than a wrong size.

items.$description: The links, with real rhythm — a small consistent gap rather than none, so the eye reads them as a list instead of as a paragraph of words.

footer.$description: Pinned to the bottom by `margin-block-start: auto`, and separated by a rule — it is not the last item in the list, it is what the list sits above.

group.$description: A titled cluster of links. What turns a flat list of nine items into three groups of three, which is the difference between scanning and reading.

group-title.$description: Composes `text--eyebrow`. Only the placement is the sidebar's.

item.$description: One link. The whole row is the target, not the text — a nav item you have to hit the words of is a nav item that misses on a trackpad. `radius-sm`, because a full pill in a vertical stack reads as a row of buttons.
item.transition: background var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out), color var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out)

count.$description: A trailing number — how many are in there. `margin-inline-start:auto` pushes it to the edge so the counts form their own column and can be compared down the list.

marker.$description: The bar beside the current item. It lived on `workbench` — a shell that has no items to mark — while this unit's `selected` state DESCRIBED a marker in prose and drew none, so the one thing that reads at a glance was documented in one unit and declared in another. Absolute against the item rather than a border on it, so it can be shorter than the row and centred: a full-height border reads as a divider, not as a marker.

drawer.$description: The same element, moved — not a second copy. `translate` rather than `display:none` so the open state can animate and the DOM keeps one landmark.

plain.$description: No fill and no rule — for a rail inside a surface that already has both.

selected.$description: The current page. A filled row AND the marker bar at its leading edge — the fill alone is a tint someone can miss on a dim screen, and the bar is the part that reads at a glance from across the room. The marker is present at `opacity: 0` on every item and revealed here, so the current item settles instead of the bar popping into existence.

reducedMotion.$description: It still opens; it just arrives. Never remove the transform itself — the drawer would then be permanently off-screen.

a11y.note: One `<nav>` with one `aria-label`, in both layouts. As a drawer it needs a focus trap while open, Escape to close, and focus returned to the control that opened it. The current item carries `aria-current=page`; it is not marked by colour alone.
